paper.title: Vaccination against measles-mumps-rubella and rates of non-targeted infectious disease hospitalisations: Nationwide register-based cohort studies in Denmark, Finland, Norway, and Sweden
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability (p. 10), verbatim: "Due to data protection rules, we are not allowed to share the individual-level data, but other researchers fulfilling the requirements could obtain similar data from the register controllers." No code …

registers.name_in_paper: national vaccination registries (Denmark: the Danish vaccination register)
registers.role: treatment — type and date of every administered DTaP, MMR, PCV, rotavirus and other vaccine

registers.name_in_paper: nationwide patient registries (Denmark: the Danish National Patient Registry)
registers.role: outcomes — all hospital contacts with diagnoses and dates of admission and discharge; ICD-10 since 1997

controls — year and season of birth, sex, birth weight, mode of delivery, maternal smoking during pregnancy, singleton, child order, maternal age, maternal origin, household income quintile, single parenthood, maternal highest attained education, number of inpatient hospital contacts before 12 months of age, chronic diseases, receipt of other live or non-live vaccines

registers.name_in_paper: the Nordic collaboration “NONSEnse” common data model (Gehrt et al., BMJ Open 2023)
registers.role: sample frame / harmonisation — the collaboration within which the data were collected and harmonised; data stored in each country separately

linkages: In all countries, the personal ID given upon birth or taking residency in the country makes linkage of data from the different registries possible.
children linked to maternal characteristics (age, origin, education, smoking during pregnancy) and to household income and single parenthood

sample.universe: All children born in Denmark and Norway from 1 January 2008, in Finland from 1 July 2010 and in Sweden from 1 January 2013, until and including 31 December 2015
sample.unit_of_observation: child (person-time, with infectious disease hospitalisations as recurrent events)
selection_rules: A total of 1,621,643 children were born in the countries during the respective study periods.
Exclude children who had received any measles-containing vaccine before 11 months of age.
Exclude children who had not received two doses of DTaP before 11 months of age.
Exclude children who had received the third dose of DTaP before 11 months of age.
Exclude children with unknown information on a variable where fewer than 2 per thousand had missing information.
1,397,027 children remained: 427,173 in Denmark, 270,059 in Finland, 441,704 in Norway and 277,385 in Sweden.
Follow-up starts at the date of vaccination (first of MMR or DTaP3) or at baseline, whichever occurred last.
Follow-up ends at 2 years of age, death, emigration, receipt of a fourth DTaP dose, a second MMR dose, or 31 December 2017, whichever occurred first.
sample.period: 2008–2017 (Finland from 2010, Sweden from 2013; follow-up to 31 December 2017)

construction_notes: Baseline is 2 weeks prior to the age of recommended MMR vaccination in Denmark, Norway and Sweden, and 2 weeks after it in Finland; it was set by visual inspection of the vaccine exposure distribution (sFigure 2) and of IPTW plots by age.
MMR is recommended at 15 months of age in Denmark and Norway, 18 months in Sweden, and at 12 months (with DTaP3) in Finland; DTaP and PCV at 3, 5 and 12 months in all countries.
Vaccination status is time-varying with five categories: DTaP3; MMR-after-DTaP3; MMR-with-DTaP3; MMR-after-DTaP2; DTaP3-after-MMR. The analysis contrasts MMR-after-DTaP3 with DTaP3.

Infectious disease hospitalisations enter as recurrent events; an event within 14 days of a previous event belongs to the same episode, so the 13-day period after each event is censored and follow-up restarts on day 14.
Crude rates are reported as the number of events per 100 person-years.

Inverse probability of treatment weights were estimated by multinomial logistic regression in 14-day age intervals and truncated above the 99th percentile; the IPTW model is further adjusted for the covariates.
Outcome categories URTI, LRTI, GI and OI are defined by ICD-10 codes listed in sMaterial 1; primary and secondary diagnoses both count.
Country-specific estimates are pooled by the DerSimonian-Laird random-effects method.
In Norway only month of birth was available; an exact date of birth was assigned as a random integer within the month of birth.
Maternal education is classified according to ISCED2011; chronic diseases according to Kristensen et al.
Analyses were run in each country separately with identical statistical code in Stata 16 and/or 17.

claims.statement: Among children in Denmark who had followed the DTaP programme to 11 months of age, having MMR after the third DTaP dose is associated with a lower rate of infectious disease hospitalisation with at least one overnight stay than having three DTaP doses and no MMR.

treatment.label: MMR vaccine given after three doses of DTaP (MMR-after-DTaP3), compared with three doses of DTaP and no MMR (DTaP3)

register_source.value: national vaccination registries (Denmark: the Danish vaccination register) — type and date of each administered vaccine; no DST variable names given

definition.value: Time-varying vaccination status that changes on the date of each DTaP or MMR vaccination after baseline; category 2) 'MMR given after three doses of DTaP (MMR-after-DTaP3)' contrasted with the reference category 1) 'three doses of DTaP (DTaP3)'. Baseline is 2 weeks before the recommended age of MMR vaccination in Denmark, Norway and Sweden and 2 weeks after it in Finland.

timing.value: date of vaccination; status time-varying over follow-up from baseline (about 14.5 months of age in Denmark and Norway, 17.5 months in Sweden, 12.5 months in Finland) until 2 years of age

outcome.label: infectious disease hospitalisation with a minimum of one overnight stay (any type of infection)

register_source.value: nationwide patient registries (Denmark: the Danish National Patient Registry, i.e. LPR); no DST variable names given

definition.value: inpatient contacts with overnight stays for any type of infection, including primary and secondary diagnoses (sMaterial 1), ICD-10 coded; included as recurrent events, with events within 14 days of a previous event counted as the same episode and the following 13 days censored

timing.value: children followed from their date of vaccination (first of MMR or DTaP3), or from baseline whichever occurred last, until 2 years of age

units.value: hazard ratio (rate of infectious disease hospitalisation in the exposed group relative to the reference group)

magnitude.interpretation: The reduction was smaller in Denmark (14%) than in the other Nordic countries (approximately 30%).

estimand.target_population: children in Denmark who had received two doses of DTaP but no third DTaP dose and no measles-containing vaccine before 11 months of age
estimand.time_horizon: children followed from their date of vaccination (first of MMR or DTaP3), or from baseline whichever occurred last, until 2 years of age

population.description: Children in Denmark, born 1 January 2008 – 31 December 2015, who had received the second dose of DTaP but neither the third DTaP dose, the first MMR dose nor any other measles-containing vaccine before 11 months of age, followed to 2 years of age.
population.ages: from baseline (2 weeks before the recommended MMR age in Denmark, Norway and Sweden; 2 weeks after it in Finland) until 2 years of age
subgroups_defined: children who had received two doses of PCV before 11 months of age and RV as recommended
population.selection: children who had received the second dose of DTaP but neither the third dose of DTaP, the first dose of MMR nor any other measles-containing vaccine before 11 months of age; children with missing information on a variable where fewer than 2 per thousand were missing were excluded

identification.source_of_variation: Observational variation, within a cohort restricted to children who followed the DTaP/MMR programme to 11 months of age, in whether and when the child had received MMR after the third DTaP dose; vaccination status enters as a time-varying exposure with age as the underlying timescale.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the measured covariates and on age (the underlying timescale), time-varying vaccination status is independent of the rate of infectious disease hospitalisation — i.e. no unmeasured confounding.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors adjust for the listed covariates, use age as the underlying timescale, repeat the analysis with inverse probability of treatment weights, and compute G-values for the confounding strength that would return the aHR to the null; they state that they cannot exclude residual confounding.

key_assumptions.assumption: Proportional hazards: the hazard ratio between vaccination groups is constant over the follow-up age range.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Tested with Schoenfeld residuals for the primary outcome in the covariate-adjusted model; non-proportional hazards were found in Norway, where HRs were re-estimated in 8-week follow-up intervals.

key_assumptions.assumption: No residual confounding from unmeasured reasons for delayed or absent vaccination (healthy vaccinee bias) — an assumption the authors explicitly say is violated to some degree.
key_assumptions.supported_by: A negative control exposure analysis (DTaP3 vs DTaP2) also showed a beneficial association, which the authors read as evidence that bias accounts for at least part of the estimate.

key_assumptions.assumption: Loss to follow-up is non-informative: children who leave the country temporarily cannot be censored, and MMR is recommended before travel, so follow-up time is conditioned on remaining registered in the country.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Subgroup analysis restricted to children with two native-born parents (sTable 7) did not substantially change the results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Positivity / overlap: every covariate stratum has a non-zero probability of each vaccination status at each 14-day age interval.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Inverse probability of treatment weights were estimated in 14-day age intervals and truncated above the 99th percentile; follow-up was limited to age intervals where a sufficient number of children had received MMR.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: one child's vaccination status does not affect another child's rate of infectious disease hospitalisation.

threats_discussed: residual confounding inherent to observational studies
healthy vaccinee bias (MMR postponed if the child has fever; MMR can give transient fever)
bias from reasons for not being vaccinated as recommended, probed with a negative control exposure
loss to follow-up from temporary emigration that cannot be censored
vaccine hesitancy indicated by missing PCV and rotavirus vaccinations
non-proportional hazards (observed in Norway)
differences in diagnostic coding practice across the four countries
higher and steeper MMR uptake implying a more selected unvaccinated group and a greater bias
robustness_checks: inverse probability of treatment weighted (IPTW) Cox model with time-varying weights, further adjusted for the covariates (right-hand panel of Figures 3–5, sTable 4)
unadjusted hazard ratios (sTable 3)
subgroup restricted to children of parents born in the respective countries (sTable 7)
censoring the 14 days after receipt of MMR (sTable 8)
censoring upon influenza vaccination in Finland (sTable 9)
restriction to children who had received two doses of PCV before 11 months of age and RV as recommended (sTable 10)
negative control exposure analysis, DTaP3 vs DTaP2 (Figure 5, sTable 11)
G-values for the strength of unmeasured confounding required to return the aHR to the null (sTable 12)
Schoenfeld-residual test of proportional hazards, with HRs re-estimated in 8-week intervals where violated (sTable 5)
unresolved_confounders: residual confounding that the authors state they cannot exclude
unmeasured reasons for delayed or absent MMR vaccination (healthy vaccinee bias), which the authors say must be suspected to account for at least some of the association in all countries

estimation.specification: Extended Cox regression, age as the underlying time scale, vaccination status as a time-varying exposure, infectious disease hospitalisations as recurrent events (Andersen-Gill), 13 days censored after each event; covariate-adjusted model. No estimating equation is printed.
controls: number of inpatient hospital contacts before 12 months of age
receipt of other live or non-live vaccines

source_table.value: Figure 3, left panel (Covariate adjusted HR), row: Denmark, 1 night

adjustment_set.label: number of inpatient hospital contacts before 12 months of age
receipt of other live or non-live vaccines
age (underlying timescale of the Cox model)

mediators_claimed: trained innate immunity — proposed, not demonstrated here: 'Trained innate immunity has been proposed as a concept and mechanism for NSEs of vaccines.'

heterogeneity.finding: Summary estimate 0.73 (0.62 to 0.84) for boys and 0.78 (0.69 to 0.87) for girls (sFigure 5); the paper reports no consistent sex-differential effects.

The reduction was smaller in Denmark (14%) than in the other Nordic countries (approximately 30%); the authors attribute the difference to the lower and less steep MMR uptake in Denmark and hence less healthy-vaccinee bias.
The summary estimate for hospitalisations with at least two overnight stays was 0.72 (0.62 to 0.82), similar to the 0.75 (0.65 to 0.84) for at least one overnight stay.

ambiguities: The point estimate is read from the left-hand (Covariate adjusted HR) panel of Figure 3; the same row of the right-hand IPTW panel prints a different number, recorded here only as a robustness check.
horizon is expressed in child age (follow-up ends at 2 years of age), not in time since vaccination, because the paper defines follow-up by age.

evidence.annotation: Hazard ratios of infectious disease hospitalisations with a minimum of 1 or 2 overnight stays among children with MMR after three doses of DTaP compared with 3 doses of DTaP without MMR, by country and combined in summary estimate.

evidence.how: The paper states MMR is recommended at 15 months in Denmark and Norway, 18 months in Sweden and 12 months in Finland, and that baseline is 2 weeks before the recommended MMR age in Denmark, Norway and Sweden and 2 weeks after it in Finland. Subtracting or adding 2 weeks gives the approximate baseline ages of 14.5, 17.5 and 12.5 months; the paper never prints these numbers.

prior_findings_compared.citation: Sorup S, Benn CS, Poulsen A, Krause TG, Aaby P, Ravn H. Live vaccine against measles, mumps, and rubella and the risk of hospital admissions for nontargeted infections. JAMA 2014;311(8):826–35.
prior_findings_compared.as_stated: The first study found an aHR of 0.86 (0.84 to 0.88),5 similar to the Danish estimates in our study (aHR: 0.86 (0.83 to 0.89))

falsification.condition: The authors pre-specify a negative control exposure (three vs two DTaP doses), for which no beneficial effect should be seen if the MMR association is causal; they report that the negative control also yielded a reduction of 19% (95% CI: 13–25%) across countries and conclude that bias accounts for at least some of the observed association.

treatment.label: MMR vaccine given after three doses of DTaP (MMR-after-DTaP3), compared with three doses of DTaP and no MMR (DTaP3)

register_source.value: national vaccination registries (Denmark: the Danish vaccination register) — type and date of each administered vaccine; no DST variable names given

definition.value: Time-varying vaccination status that changes on the date of each DTaP or MMR vaccination after baseline; category 2) 'MMR given after three doses of DTaP (MMR-after-DTaP3)' contrasted with the reference category 1) 'three doses of DTaP (DTaP3)'. Baseline is 2 weeks before the recommended age of MMR vaccination in Denmark, Norway and Sweden and 2 weeks after it in Finland.

timing.value: date of vaccination; status time-varying over follow-up from baseline (about 14.5 months of age in Denmark and Norway, 17.5 months in Sweden, 12.5 months in Finland) until 2 years of age

outcome.label: infectious disease hospitalisation with at least two overnight stays (any type of infection)

register_source.value: nationwide patient registries (Denmark: the Danish National Patient Registry, i.e. LPR); no DST variable names given

definition.value: inpatient contacts with at least two overnight stays for any type of infection (representing the more severe infections), ICD-10 coded; recurrent events with the same 14-day episode rule

timing.value: children followed from their date of vaccination (first of MMR or DTaP3), or from baseline whichever occurred last, until 2 years of age

units.value: hazard ratio (rate of infectious disease hospitalisation in the exposed group relative to the reference group)

estimand.target_population: children in Finland who had received two doses of DTaP but no third DTaP dose and no measles-containing vaccine before 11 months of age
estimand.time_horizon: children followed from their date of vaccination (first of MMR or DTaP3), or from baseline whichever occurred last, until 2 years of age

population.description: Children in Finland, born 1 July 2010 – 31 December 2015, who had received the second dose of DTaP but neither the third DTaP dose, the first MMR dose nor any other measles-containing vaccine before 11 months of age, followed to 2 years of age.
population.ages: from baseline (2 weeks before the recommended MMR age in Denmark, Norway and Sweden; 2 weeks after it in Finland) until 2 years of age
subgroups_defined: children who had received two doses of PCV before 11 months of age and RV as recommended
population.selection: children who had received the second dose of DTaP but neither the third dose of DTaP, the first dose of MMR nor any other measles-containing vaccine before 11 months of age; children with missing information on a variable where fewer than 2 per thousand were missing were excluded

identification.source_of_variation: Observational variation, within a cohort restricted to children who followed the DTaP/MMR programme to 11 months of age, in whether and when the child had received MMR after the third DTaP dose; vaccination status enters as a time-varying exposure with age as the underlying timescale.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the measured covariates and on age (the underlying timescale), time-varying vaccination status is independent of the rate of infectious disease hospitalisation — i.e. no unmeasured confounding.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors adjust for the listed covariates, use age as the underlying timescale, repeat the analysis with inverse probability of treatment weights, and compute G-values for the confounding strength that would return the aHR to the null; they state that they cannot exclude residual confounding.

key_assumptions.assumption: Proportional hazards: the hazard ratio between vaccination groups is constant over the follow-up age range.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Tested with Schoenfeld residuals for the primary outcome in the covariate-adjusted model; non-proportional hazards were found in Norway, where HRs were re-estimated in 8-week follow-up intervals.

key_assumptions.assumption: No residual confounding from unmeasured reasons for delayed or absent vaccination (healthy vaccinee bias) — an assumption the authors explicitly say is violated to some degree.
key_assumptions.supported_by: A negative control exposure analysis (DTaP3 vs DTaP2) also showed a beneficial association, which the authors read as evidence that bias accounts for at least part of the estimate.

key_assumptions.assumption: Loss to follow-up is non-informative: children who leave the country temporarily cannot be censored, and MMR is recommended before travel, so follow-up time is conditioned on remaining registered in the country.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Subgroup analysis restricted to children with two native-born parents (sTable 7) did not substantially change the results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Positivity / overlap: every covariate stratum has a non-zero probability of each vaccination status at each 14-day age interval.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Inverse probability of treatment weights were estimated in 14-day age intervals and truncated above the 99th percentile; follow-up was limited to age intervals where a sufficient number of children had received MMR.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: one child's vaccination status does not affect another child's rate of infectious disease hospitalisation.

healthy vaccinee bias (MMR postponed if the child has fever; MMR can give transient fever)
bias from reasons for not being vaccinated as recommended, probed with a negative control exposure

vaccine hesitancy indicated by missing PCV and rotavirus vaccinations
non-proportional hazards (observed in Norway)
differences in diagnostic coding practice across the four countries
higher and steeper MMR uptake implying a more selected unvaccinated group and a greater bias

unadjusted hazard ratios (sTable 3)
subgroup restricted to children of parents born in the respective countries (sTable 7)
censoring the 14 days after receipt of MMR (sTable 8)
censoring upon influenza vaccination in Finland (sTable 9)

negative control exposure analysis, DTaP3 vs DTaP2 (Figure 5, sTable 11)

unmeasured reasons for delayed or absent MMR vaccination (healthy vaccinee bias), which the authors say must be suspected to account for at least some of the association in all countries

estimation.specification: Extended Cox regression, age as the underlying time scale, vaccination status as a time-varying exposure, infectious disease hospitalisations as recurrent events (Andersen-Gill), 13 days censored after each event; covariate-adjusted model. No estimating equation is printed.
controls: number of inpatient hospital contacts before 12 months of age
receipt of other live or non-live vaccines

heterogeneity.finding: Summary estimate 0.73 (0.62 to 0.84) for boys and 0.78 (0.69 to 0.87) for girls (sFigure 5); the paper reports no consistent sex-differential effects.

The reduction was smaller in Denmark (14%) than in the other Nordic countries (approximately 30%); the authors attribute the difference to the lower and less steep MMR uptake in Denmark and hence less healthy-vaccinee bias.

ambiguities: The country-level 2-night hazard ratios are printed only in Figure 3 (and sTable 3, not in this PDF); the running text gives the summary estimate alone.
The point estimate is read from the left-hand (Covariate adjusted HR) panel of Figure 3.

evidence.annotation: Hazard ratios of infectious disease hospitalisations with a minimum of 1 or 2 overnight stays among children with MMR after three doses of DTaP compared with 3 doses of DTaP without MMR, by country and combined in summary estimate.

evidence.how: The paper states MMR is recommended at 15 months in Denmark and Norway, 18 months in Sweden and 12 months in Finland, and that baseline is 2 weeks before the recommended MMR age in Denmark, Norway and Sweden and 2 weeks after it in Finland. Subtracting or adding 2 weeks gives the approximate baseline ages of 14.5, 17.5 and 12.5 months; the paper never prints these numbers.

falsification.condition: The authors pre-specify a negative control exposure (three vs two DTaP doses), for which no beneficial effect should be seen if the MMR association is causal; they report that the negative control also yielded a reduction of 19% (95% CI: 13–25%) across countries and conclude that bias accounts for at least some of the observed association.

evidence.how: The paper states MMR is recommended at 15 months in Denmark and Norway, 18 months in Sweden and 12 months in Finland, and that baseline is 2 weeks before the recommended MMR age in Denmark, Norway and Sweden and 2 weeks after it in Finland. Subtracting or adding 2 weeks gives the approximate baseline ages of 14.5, 17.5 and 12.5 months; the paper never prints these numbers.

falsification.condition: The authors pre-specify a negative control exposure (three vs two DTaP doses), for which no beneficial effect should be seen if the MMR association is causal; they report that the negative control also yielded a reduction of 19% (95% CI: 13–25%) across countries and conclude that bias accounts for at least some of the observed association.
